written.myAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant. Its types are stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.
Transpiration creates a pull in the xylem that helps transport water and mineral salts from roots to leaves.
Transpiration is a necessary evil. It creates a pull in the xylem, helping transport water and mineral salts from roots to leaves.
Lenticular transpiration is water-vapour loss through lenticels, usually in stems. Stomatal transpiration is water-vapour loss through stomata, mainly in leaves, and accounts for most transpiration.

In daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, raising their solute concentration. Water enters by osmosis, making them turgid and opening the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions move out and the solute concentration falls; water leaves by osmosis, the guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes.
Higher temperature increases transpiration by speeding evaporation. Wind increases it by carrying away humid air around leaves. High humidity decreases it by reducing the water-vapour gradient.
Wind carries humid air away from leaves, allowing more water to evaporate and increasing transpiration. High humidity reduces transpiration.
